Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 48
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Rabbi
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds, Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed, Media / News: Related news
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others, Avoid Sex: Sex, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore

Vignette:
Imani was forty-five when the bomb shattered the Saturday morning service. She had been at the bimah, midway through the Torah reading, when the blast came from the rear of the sanctuary—a deafening crack that folded the air and threw her to the floor. For a long moment there was only ringing and dust. Then the screaming began. She crawled toward the back, toward the broken bodies, but by the time she reached the doorway the first responders were already pushing her away. In the weeks that followed, the congregation held her up as a hero for staying calm, for leading the survivors out. Imani did not feel like a hero. She replayed the moment again and again: the split second before the explosion when she had heard something—a scrape, a footstep—and had not turned. If she had turned, if she had shouted, if she had done something, maybe the man with the backpack would not have made it inside. She told herself this so often that the thought became a kind of prayer, except there was no comfort in it. She would never forgive herself for not doing more to stop what happened.

At first the symptoms were easy to explain away. She was tired, she was grieving, she was carrying the weight of her community. But the sound of a car backfiring on the street outside her study made her drop a coffee cup. The bang from a collapsing shelf in the supply closet sent her to her knees. She began to avoid the parts of the synagogue where the damage had been worst, then the entire rear hallway, then any room without a clear exit. Her husband, David, would find her standing at the kitchen window at two in the morning, watching the street. She told him she needed to be sure no one was out there. At night the fear sharpened; the darkness seemed to hide a thousand possible threats, and she could not make herself believe that the doors were locked, that the house was safe, even when he showed her each bolt. She started scanning everywhere—parking lots, grocery aisles, the corridor between her office and the sanctuary. Every face could be the face of someone watching her, waiting. The sensation of being observed followed her even into her own home. She stopped answering the phone when the news came on, and when a member of the congregation mentioned a new report about the attacker’s trial, Imani left the room without excusing herself.

The change that frightened her most was in her marriage. Before the bombing, sex had been a source of comfort and connection. Now the thought of being that vulnerable—exposed, undressed, unaware—made her chest tighten. She offered excuses: a headache, late work, exhaustion. David was patient, but she saw the hurt in his eyes and could not explain that it was not about him. It was about the feeling that any moment something terrible could happen, and she had to stay ready. She had come to believe that letting her guard down was a betrayal of the vigilance she owed herself and everyone around her. Nothing good could happen to her anymore. The future that had once felt full of possibility now felt like a corridor with no end, only more scanning, more waiting, more guilt.

Her work suffered in quieter ways. She had always been a pastor who visited the sick, sat with the grieving, led with empathy. Now she found herself hurrying through hospital hallways, her eyes darting from door to door, unable to focus on the person in the bed. She stopped attending evening meetings because the drive home after dark felt too dangerous. Her senior staff noticed but attributed it to trauma, which made Imani feel both grateful and ashamed. She was a Rabbi. She was supposed to help others make meaning out of suffering, but she could no longer find meaning in her own life.

What finally brought her to seek help was a small thing. David said, during a quiet argument about her avoiding yet another family dinner, “You’re not even here when you’re here.” She heard the grief in his voice, and for a moment she saw herself through his eyes—a woman always scanning, always bracing, never truly present. She agreed to see a therapist because she was terrified of losing him, and even more terrified that she had already lost herself. What she hoped for, though she could barely admit it, was to one day walk into a room without checking the exits first. To feel safe enough to close her eyes at night. To believe, even for a second, that the world was not waiting to explode.
